A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Information-Driven Design of Imaging Systems. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and complete supplementary materials support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v4 reports original estimator-validation experiments, four imaging applications, IDEAL optimization results, and supplementary simulations and analyses.

after.justification: v5 retains these original empirical results and additionally presents a direct IDEAL versus end-to-end comparison in Figure 3c.

M1.justification: The three implemented estimators and demonstrated IDEAL procedure remain unchanged. Sections S2.7–S2.8 introduce proposed extensions involving object-conditioned calibration and weighted task-specific information objectives; these are not presented as experimentally validated replacements.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same photography, black-hole imaging, lensless reconstruction/classification, microscopy, MNIST, and synthetic validation coverage. Quantum imaging and privacy-related applications in v5 are proposed directions, not evaluated scenarios.

E2.justification: Figure 3c adds Chakrabarti's end-to-end color-filter design as a direct comparator to IDEAL. This learned design already participated in the Figure 2 photography comparison, but was absent from v4's optimization-stage comparison.

E3.justification: The detailed experimental splits, preprocessing, metrics, model configurations, and training budgets in S6 remain unchanged. The added Figure 3 comparator does not introduce a separately specified evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: Figure 3c drops the intermediate optimization stage's PixelCNN-information and reconstruction-error point, reducing the displayed validation of optimization progress while retaining initial/final results and the optimization curve. Supplementary sensitivity, consistency, noise, and classification analyses remain.

E5.justification: The bootstrap procedures, replicate information, confidence levels, and training-time uncertainty reporting are retained. Figure 3's revised comparison uses the existing 95% confidence reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figure 3c replaces the intermediate-stage result with an end-to-end result and reports comparable final IDEAL performance. Other benchmark and supplementary results are retained. Section 3 newly states a roughly 20-photon failure threshold, without reconciling it with S3.5's retained roughly 40-photon discussion.

T1.justification: v5 adds a proof of the deterministic information-transfer equality and substantially revises the stochastic-encoder formalism, alongside new task-information decompositions and weighted objectives. S2.7 introduces an incorrect chain-rule identity: its defined average I(O;Y|E) must be combined with I(E;Y), whereas the paper combines it with I(E;Y|O).

C1.justification: The abstract, IDEAL section, and discussion newly claim that IDEAL matches end-to-end optimization performance. v4 claimed successful optimization and potential computational advantages without this direct parity claim. The central measurement-based information-estimation contribution remains.

C2.justification: v5 distinguishes information lost through encoder variation from additional measurement diversity, emphasizes object-dependent calibration difficulties, and explicitly excludes quantum imaging from the present treatment. It also adds an argument about robustness to object-independent noise-model errors. Existing task-specific limitations remain.

D1.justification: Section 3 newly reports a general working range of approximately 1,000–10,000 patches of roughly 20×20 pixels. This adds a summary disclosure; the detailed S6 implementation recipes, hardware information, and code-access instructions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v5 adds subsequent information-driven optical-design and Bayesian-optimization work and three quantum-metrology references. It removes the CIDRE and BaSiC illumination-correction citations. The broader positioning against estimation theory and compressed sensing remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and most main-text sections are extensively rewritten and reorganized. IDEAL becomes numbered Section 5, discussion becomes Section 6 with explicit future-direction headings, and supplementary material on encoder uncertainty and task information is reorganized into S2.7–S2.8.

P2.justification: A new Table 1 summarizes previously described model properties and training times. Figures 1–3 receive revised sizing, labels, captions, and diagram arrangements, including the changed Figure 3c comparison. All 23 supplementary figures retain their drawing content, with some relocation.

improvement.justification: v5 improves organization, adds a useful direct end-to-end comparison, and supplies an explicit deterministic-encoding proof. However, its new S2.7 chain-rule error undermines the proposed stochastic-encoder correction, and the new low-photon threshold is inconsistent with the retained appendix discussion. These correctness problems outweigh the limited evidential gains, while the unchanged core estimator and experiments limit the overall deterioration.
